blogs.title: When Do Threats Become ‘Persecution’? The Tenth Circuit Draws a Hard Line in Jimenez v. Bondi
blogs.description: This post unpacks the court’s past-persecution analysis, highlighting the Tenth Circuit’s insistence that threats—even repeated, gunpoint threats coupled with emotional trauma and an attempted intimidation of a child—generally do not suffice without more. Relying on precedents like Karki and Wiransane, the panel emphasizes cumulative assessment but still finds no persecution where there was no lasting physical harm and the incidents did not rise beyond menacing threats. We contrast this approach with other circuits that have sometimes treated sustained, specific death threats as persecution in narrow circumstances, and we explore how substantial-evidence deference makes reversals unlikely. The takeaway for practitioners is the need to develop records showing concrete harm or restraints, sustained pattern severity, and objective indicators of imminent violence rather than psychological impact alone.

blogs.title: Politics or Policing? Parsing Nexus and the ‘Snitch’ Motive in Mixed-Motive Asylum Claims
blogs.description: Jimenez spotlights the difficulty of proving political nexus where private criminals perceive an applicant as a threat to their enterprise. The court, applying the “at least one central reason” standard, treats the persecutors’ references to the petitioners as “snitches for the police” and “in politics” as evidence of a primarily anti-informant motive, not a political one—especially given the escalation after the property dispute tied to Don Rafa’s operation. The panel underscores gaps in tying earlier politically infused threats to the later, identified persecutor and notes that the petitioners did not meaningfully brief a particular-social-group theory based on informant status. We examine how timing, statements by persecutors, and motive parsing operate in mixed-motive cases after O.C.V. v. Bondi, and we offer practice tips on preserving alternative nexus theories and marshaling proof that political opinion is more than tangential.

blogs.title: Reporting as Gatekeeping: The ‘Unable or Unwilling’ Test After Singh v. Bondi
blogs.description: On government protection, the panel doubles down on Singh’s framework: whether authorities tried to stop the persecutors and whether they offered the applicant protection, with notice to the government as a key predicate. Here, the petitioners’ minimal outreach (two discouraging conversations with officers) and the record of prior police searches at the property undercut claims of governmental complicity or impotence. The court treats a single unhelpful officer as insufficient to show systemic failure and rejects futility or danger as unsupported by the evidence presented. For litigants, the message is clear: file reports where feasible or robustly document why doing so would be dangerous; substantiate systemic corruption or collusion beyond isolated anecdotes; and align country-conditions evidence with on-the-ground efforts (or credible reasons for their absence).

blogs.title: Internal Relocation by Anecdote: Three Weeks in the Countryside and the Reasonableness Inquiry
blogs.description: The court’s relocation analysis leans on pragmatic indicia: the threats urged the family to leave the neighborhood (not the country), relatives remain unharmed, and the family spent three uneventful weeks in the countryside before departing. Absent past persecution—and with a private persecutor—the applicant generally bears the burden to show relocation is unreasonable, a showing the panel finds lacking here. The opinion also faults “haphazard” briefing on economic, administrative, and infrastructure barriers, despite regulations that list reasonableness factors like those in 8 C.F.R. § 1208.13(b)(3). We explore whether short-term safety should carry outsized weight, how to build a record on persecutor reach and feasibility of relocation, and the importance of preserving granular arguments about reasonableness rather than relying on generalized assertions.
